title: India Just Launched Two Anti-Dumping Probes in One Week. One Could Make Its Own Power Grid More Expensive.
excerpt: New Delhi is cracking down on cheap steel from China, Japan, and Russia — but duties on transformer-grade electrical steel could slow a ₹9 lakh crore grid expansion that India can't afford to delay.
body:
India's trade ministry has opened two separate anti-dumping investigations in a single week — one targeting hot-rolled flat steel from China, Japan, and Russia, and another aimed at transformer-grade electrical steel from China, Japan, South Korea, and Russia. Together, they represent New Delhi's most aggressive trade-defence action in years. But the second probe has set off alarm bells across the power sector, where experts warn that duties on a material India can barely produce at home could raise transformer costs and slow the country's most ambitious infrastructure programme.

The Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR), the commerce ministry's investigative arm, issued the hot-rolled steel notification on Thursday after a joint application from JSW Steel, JSW Vijayanagar Metallics, and Jindal Steel Odisha. Tata Steel and the Steel Authority of India have thrown their weight behind the petition. The companies allege that dumped imports — Chinese steel that undercuts domestic prices by anywhere from $11 to $37 a tonne — have caused material injury and threaten further harm. They want duties applied retroactively.

The numbers tell a clear story. China's finished steel exports to India more than doubled in April to the highest level in at least two years, reaching roughly 232,000 metric tonnes. Despite a three-year safeguard duty of 12 per cent that New Delhi imposed in December to curb cheap Chinese shipments, India remained a net steel importer for the second straight month in May. Imports of finished steel hit 700,000 tonnes, well above the six-month average.

"The applicants have claimed that the volume of imports increased in both absolute terms and in relation to demand in India over the injury period," the DGTR notification states. The domestic industry reported rising inventories, suppressed prices, declining margins, and falling return on investments.

But it is the second investigation — into cold-rolled grain-oriented (CRGO) electrical steel and amorphous metals — that has trade economists worried. CRGO is the specialised steel used in the magnetic cores of every power and distribution transformer in the country. India consumes between 400,000 and 450,000 tonnes of it annually. Domestic production, from India's only manufacturer — JSW JFE Electrical Steel Nashik, the company that filed the complaint — is just 40,000 to 50,000 tonnes. Nearly 90 per cent of India's CRGO requirement is imported.

"The move has raised concerns that imposing anti-dumping duties on a product for which India imports nearly 90 per cent of its requirements could increase transformer costs and slow the country's ambitious power-grid expansion," said Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) and a former Indian Trade Service officer.

India is investing ₹9.15 lakh crore to expand its power grid by 2032, adding 191,000 circuit kilometres of transmission lines and more than doubling transformer capacity to 2,342 gigavolt-amperes. That buildout depends on an uninterrupted supply of affordable CRGO. Higher duties could raise prices without reducing import dependence, potentially stalling investments in transmission infrastructure, renewable energy integration, and distribution networks.

Srivastava also questioned the investigation's methodology. The DGTR is treating China as a non-market economy and citing a lack of domestic price data for Japan, South Korea, and Russia, effectively benchmarking all four against India's own production costs. "Exporters from four different economies are being assessed against the same Indian cost benchmark," GTRI noted — a practice that, critics say, risks inflating the calculated dumping margin.

The probe covers imports from April 2025 to March 2026, while the injury analysis spans 2022-23 to 2024-25. India currently excludes CRGO from safeguard duties precisely because of the country's overwhelming import dependence. Every imported coil must also carry Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certification, making this a pricing dispute, not a quality one.

For India's steel majors — JSW, Tata, SAIL, and Jindal — the hot-rolled probe offers a shield they've lobbied for. But the CRGO case puts New Delhi in a bind. Protect the country's only electrical steel producer and risk making every new transformer more expensive, or keep imports cheap and watch that lone manufacturer struggle against subsidised foreign competitors.

India's government has said it will monitor steel imports for at least two more months before deciding on further measures. In the meantime, it has also separately requested the finance ministry withdraw a provisional anti-dumping duty on low-ash metallurgical coke, a key steelmaking raw material, to keep domestic supply costs manageable.

The larger picture is stark. As India races to electrify, decarbonise, and industrialise, it is running headlong into a dilemma that developing economies know well: the tension between protecting domestic producers and keeping the inputs for national infrastructure affordable. In steel, both sides of that argument now have an active investigation to cite.
nri_angle: India's ₹9 lakh crore power grid expansion — which NRI investors have poured into through infrastructure bonds and mutual funds — could face higher costs if anti-dumping duties raise transformer steel prices, while the trade crackdown on Chinese steel signals shifting investment dynamics in India's manufacturing sector.
author: Diaspora Desk
